title: Microsoft Copilot: What Does Your License Cover and what not.
description: trying to make sense of Microsoft Copilot licensing and Copilot credits.
bodyHtml:
Microsoft Copilot licensing is getting very confusing.

We have Copilot Chat, the paid Copilot license, Agent Builder, Copilot Studio and Copilot Credits.

And after Microsoft Ignite 2026, there are more things to figure out. Cowork, Code, Autopilot and several new features that may come with extra costs.

I am trying to understand what is included in a Copilot license and when you need to pay for usage.

So I started looking through Microsoft's licensing documentation and the announcements from Ignite.

Here's what I found so far.


First, Copilot Chat

If your company has an eligible Microsoft 365 subscription, you already have access to Copilot Chat.

You can ask questions, write text, summarize documents and work with files you upload.

You can also use certain agents without extra usage charges.

For example, a simple agent that follows instructions or uses public websites may be available without Copilot Credits.

But what if you connect an agent to SharePoint?

That's where licensing gets a little more complicated.

If someone without the paid Copilot license uses an agent that accesses company data, the organization may be charged Copilot Credits.

So even though Copilot Chat is included, that doesn't mean every agent you use inside Copilot Chat is free.

What about the paid Copilot license?

With the paid Microsoft Copilot license, you get Copilot in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams and other supported Microsoft 365 apps.

You can also use some Copilot Studio agents without extra credit charges.

That 's interesting..

Because when you build an agent in Copilot Studio, you normally have to think about credits and usage.

But Microsoft includes some agent usage for employees who have a paid Copilot license.

There are conditions, though.

The agent needs to run in an eligible scenario, using the licensed employee's identity.

If you build an agent that runs automatically, or one that customers outside your company use, different billing rules can apply.

So having a paid Copilot license doesn't mean every agent you build is covered.

And then we have Copilot Credits

Copilot Credits are used to charge for certain activities.And that list keeps growing!

In Copilot Studio, different activities have different rates.

Here are some examples:

ActivityCopilot Credits
Classic answer1
Generative answer2
Agent action5
Tenant graph grounding10
Agent flow actions13 per 100 actions
Content processing8 per page

One question can use more than one activity.

For example, an agent might use tenant graph grounding and then generate an answer.

That could mean 12 credits for one interaction.

And if you use a reasoning model, token-based charges may also apply.

This is something I think is easy to miss when you're testing an agent.

You might run it a few times and see very little usage. But what happens when 200 employees start using it every day?

How do you actually pay for credits?

There are different options.

Pay-as-you-go

You connect your Power Platform environment to an Azure subscription using a billing policy.

You pay for the usage that gets billed.

For testing, this seems like a reasonable place to start, especially when you don't know how much an agent will be used.

Prepaid credits

You can also buy Copilot Credit capacity in advance.

There are many ways to buy it, including a one-year prepurchase option for eligible services.

The thing to remember is that a user license and Copilot Credits are separate.

The license covers certain features and usage.

Credits are used when an activity is charged separately.

So what changed at Ignite 2026?

Quite a few Copilot features were announced.

I'm mainly looking at the ones that affect how people use Copilot and what that might mean for licensing and costs.

Home and Office in Copilot

Microsoft introduced a new Home experience that brings Chat and Cowork together.

You can also work with Word, Excel and PowerPoint files directly inside Copilot.

That sounds useful, especially if you prefer working in one place instead of switching between apps.

But I'd still check which features are included in your license. The new interface doesn't automatically mean everything inside it has the same billing rules.

Cowork, Code and Autopilot

These are worth looking at separately.

Cowork can help with tasks that involve several steps.

Code is aimed at creating applications and working with code.

Autopilot is designed for work that can continue with less input from the user.

Some advanced usage can be charged through Copilot Credits.

Exactly what gets charged depends on the feature, task and billing rules.

So I wouldn't assume that having a paid Copilot license gives you unlimited use of all three.

Microsoft also announced Auto, which can select a model and reasoning level based on what you're asking Copilot to do.

I'm interested to see how that works in practice, especially when cost becomes part of the decision.

Today Brief and Today Feed

These two are easy to confuse.

Today Brief gives you a daily overview of things that may need your attention.

Today Feed is meant to provide more ongoing, personalized updates.

The licensing difference is worth checking.

Microsoft has described Today Brief as part of the paid Copilot experience, while Today Feed has been announced with usage-based billing in private preview.

So I wouldn't treat them as the same feature when looking at costs.

Agent 365 Cost Management

This is probably one of the more useful announcements for anyone managing Copilot and agents.

Microsoft announced more ways to see and control AI spending.

That includes usage reporting, spending limits and alerts across supported services.

I can see why this would be useful when companies start building more agents.

Right now, it's quite easy to focus on whether an agent works and leave the cost question until later.

Some of the new cost management features are still in preview, so availability will depend on your tenant.

What would I check before building an agent?

I would start with a few questions.

  • Who will use the agent?

  • Do they have a paid Copilot license?

  • Does it use company data?

  • Will it run automatically?

  • Which models, tools and actions will it use?

  • How can I see what it costs?

And before putting it into production, I'd test it with realistic usage.

Not just five questions to see if it works.

So what now?

I'm still processing some of these licensing rules, especially with the new features Microsoft keeps adding.

But one thing is becoming clearer.

We need to look beyond the Copilot license itself.

Who uses the agent, what it does and how it runs can all affect the cost.

And before choosing an agent or a billing option, I'd still start with the process or problem we're trying to solve.

I'm curious how others are handling this.

Are you already measuring Copilot Credit usage for your agents? And do you find Microsoft's licensing rules clear enough to work out the costs before building something?
